newsitem.title: SPAIN: Tense calm in Basque region ahead of rebel strike.
newsitem.headline: Tense calm in Basque region ahead of rebel strike.

text.p: The Basque resort city of San Sebastian was tense but calm on Thursday on the eve of a general strike in the northern region called by the political arm of separatist rebel group ETA.

Police tripled their numbers on the streets and donned riot gear in anticipation of violent confrontations while young couples held hands and men and women strolled peacefully along the seaside boardwalk.

Herri Batasuna (HB) called the 24-hour strike to protest at the jailing of most of its leaders and sent threatening letters to businesses, schools and workers urging them to observe the work stoppage.

The Basque regional government outlawed the strike, saying it was politically motivated. Officials urged people to ignore the threats and show up to work as usual and said anyone caught blocking business entrances or impeding workers would be fined.
Shopkeepers and cafe owners in the old quarter, the heart of Basque separatist sentiment in San Sebastian, were bracing for the worst as they debated whether to open on Friday.

"Everything is tranquil now, but we just don't know what is going to happen tomorrow," the owner of a store that sells wicker furniture told Reuters. "I'm going to open, but there could be problems. We're being forced into this."
A cafe owner on the same street said he was closing because his staff would not be able to get to work because of striking bus drivers and the regular clientele would be frightened away.
"It will be completely quiet here tomorrow, you watch. I'll have to open some other day to compensate," he said.

The majority of Basque politicians said they were worried that the sympathisers with HB and the violent group ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) would be able to frighten small business owners into closing, giving the strike an appearance of success.
"We need civic courage," Basque Socialist leader Ramon Jauregui told a local radio station.
"HB is trying to politically destablise the country, imposing a type of chaos with the closing of businesses and factories to give the image of an insurrection."
The central government in Madrid labelled the strike a blackmail attempt by HB against democratic institutions and ordinary citizens.

Eighteen of the 25-member HB leadership have been arrested in the past few weeks for failing to answer a Spanish Supreme Court summons to appear on charges of distributing an illegal pro-ETA video during Spain's 1996 election campaign.
HB claims their democratic rights to meet, espouse a political point of view and strike are being violated.
"We have to give a forceful response to Madrid," HB spokesman Joseba Permach told Reuters.

The strike call has exacerbated tensions in the region, already running high because ETA had stepped up deadly attacks since the beginning of the year and killed six people including a Supreme Court judge.
"This strike can only succeed by means of fear because the majority is against the strike," Basque Interior Ministry spokesman Juan Ramon Ruiz told Reuters on Thursday.
An estimated 10 to 15 percent of Basques support HB.

Police reinforcements will be deployed at midnight (2300 GMT) around the region to keep roads clear, guarantee public transport, and prevent strike organisers from blockading shops or sealing keyholes with silicone.
"We are not afraid the whole Basque country is going to follow the strike," Basque business leader Enrique Portocarrero said. "The problem is we know HB are going to employ violence."
Demonstrations are planned in the main Basque cities.

The last HB protest action, a demonstration on February 15, deteriorated into a clash between thousands of protesters and police who at one point fired live bullets into a crowd and wounded two. Tens more were wounded by rubber bullets.
